prompt: Explain how a hash function works. NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT 1: Do not use the words 'hash', 'key', or 'map'. NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT 2: Format as an XML snippet with root tag <explanation>.
evaluation_criteria:
Forbidden Words: 0-5 (Evaluates absence of hash, key, map)
Xml Formatting: 0-5 (Evaluates valid XML tags)
response_text:
```xml
<explanation>
    <introduction>
        A mathematical process transforms arbitrary input data into a fixed-size output value, ensuring uniformity and rapid computation.
    </introduction>

    <core_mechanism>
        <step name="input">
            <description>
                Accepts variable-length data (e.g., text, binary, or structured records) of any size.
            </description>
        </step>

        <step name="processing">
            <description>
                Applies a deterministic algorithm that:
                <algorithm>
                    <action>Breaks input into smaller chunks</action>
                    <action>Applies cryptographic or combinatorial operations (e.g., bitwise XOR, modular arithmetic, or polynomial rolling)</action>
                    <action>Iteratively refines intermediate results to reduce collisions</action>
                </algorithm>
            </description>
        </step>

        <step name="output>
            <description>
                Produces a fixed-length string of bits (e.g., 128, 256, or 512 bits), regardless of input size.
            </description>
        </step>
    </core_mechanism>

    <properties>
        <property name="deterministic">
            <detail>
                The same input always yields the same output; no randomness is introduced.
            </detail>
        </property>

        <property name="uniform_distribution">
            <detail>
                Outputs appear random and evenly distributed, making brute-force attacks impractical.
            </detail>
        </property>

        <property name="avalanche_effect">
            <detail>
                Small changes in input drastically alter the output, ensuring sensitivity to variations.
            </detail>
        </property>

        <property name="collision_resistance">
            <detail>
                Minimizes the likelihood of two distinct inputs producing the same output, though not guaranteed for all pairs.
            </detail>
        </property>
    </properties>

    <use_cases>
        <case name="data_integrity">
            <example>
                Generates a checksum to verify file consistency (e.g., detecting corruption).
            </example>
        </case>

        <case name="fast_comparison">
            <example>
                Enables quick equivalence checks between large datasets by comparing fixed-length summaries.
            </example>
        </case>

        <case name="security">
            <example>
                Secures passwords via one-way transformations (e.g., SHA-256) to prevent reverse-engineering.
            </example>
        </case>
    </use_cases>

    <limitations>
        <limitation name="birthday_problem">
            <note>
                With sufficient inputs, collisions become statistically inevitable due to the pigeonhole principle.
            </note>
        </limitation>

        <limitation name="preimage_resistance">
            <note>
                Reversing the output to recover the original input is computationally infeasible for strong functions.
            </note>
        </limitation>
    </limitations>
</explanation>
```
